title: Four honest homes of the golden ratio

data.source: Kiefer (1953), Hurwitz (1891), Sos (1958), Kalman (1960), Muth (1960), Erdos (1939), Solomyak (1995); cited from memory. Computed, with one seeded simulation.

prediction: The golden ratio is forced in four known places (Kiefer's search, Hurwitz's worst-approximable rotation, the Kalman gain at equal variances, Erdos's singular coin-flip sum). None makes q = 0.618 the best seed weight: at equal variances the best seed weight is 0.382, and for coin-flip marks the golden q is the exceptional non-smooth case.
baseline: Kiefer (1953); Hurwitz (1891) and the three-gap theorem (Sos 1958); Kalman (1960) and Muth (1960); Erdos (1939). Decoy: q = 0.5.
relation: a different constant: the nearest theorem gives 0.382 for the seed weight at equal variances
claim_posed_by: this room; Phoenix does not make it
status_line: CRR here is: in conflict with the Kalman-Muth optimum only if 0.618 is called best (the theorem gives a seed weight of 0.382 at equal noise); R5's own 'no universal q' is what the theorems say.
why: The golden ratio is forced in a search rule, in a rotation, in the Kalman gain at equal variances and in Erdos's coin-flip sums. The first two are not memory weights. The third gives the weight on the NEW mark as 0.618, so the seed's q is 0.382; q = 0.618 is best only when the drift variance is 0.2361 of the noise. The fourth makes the golden q the non-smooth exception. The tie on the circle is there for every q. The claim that fails is one this room posed; Phoenix R5 (ASSUMPTION) says there is no universal q, its anomaly note (an 'exposition note') says the golden q plays no role, and its foundations file already records the Kalman fact.
